opener.heading: Week 6: Little Bakery 🥐
about: Four things make bread, and she counts them on her fingers on Friday morning before anything goes in the bowl: flour, water, salt, yeast. The rest of the week takes them apart one at a time. The yeast gets its own jar and then its own balloon, the dough gets punched flat and stretched until it tears, and the same lump comes back as rolls, a pizza base and a tray of cinnamon buns. She follows one loop all week, from dry powder foaming in warm water to a hollow knock on the bottom of a crust.

No holiday lands in this week, so the shape comes from the theme. Four days run on a hot oven, three of them on real dough. Monday and Wednesday run on playdough, paper and a pretend shop counter, and they sit there to give your kitchen a day off. Thursday takes the whole thing out of the house: she boxes what she baked, walks a round she scouted that morning, and hands it over at four front doors.
azlyn: Yeast is alive and it eats. A jar of foam at eight thirty, a balloon standing up by eleven thirty, and an hour of waiting she can see the point of.
Hands that knead, roll, cut and press. Ten minutes of heavy work at the table on Friday, a rolling pin on Monday, and floss pulled through a log of dough on Thursday.
Her own words hold still on paper. She dictates a recipe, you read it back the same way twice, and by Thursday she picks butter out of the page on her own.
Words for what her mouth finds. Soft, chewy, seedy, holey. Five breads on five numbered plates and one word each.
Numbers doing a job. Twelve pastries counted onto a tray, a price written on every one, buttons counted into the register and back out at closing.
you: Auditory attention is trainable, and it underpins reading
Dictated stories are the bridge to real literacy
Cabin fever is a real physiological thing, not a bad attitude
Pretend play is where self-control gets built
Regression during illness is expected, not a setback
Boredom on the mend is a good sign, and a useful one
On the days you use this page instead of the plan
shopping: Salt, 500 g (a full cup of it goes into Monday's playdough)
Active dry yeast, 6 packets of 7 g
Butter, 250 g (100 g soft for Saturday, 75 g soft for Thursday)
Her chosen additions: raisins, chocolate chips, cocoa, sprinkles or a banana
Tomato sauce, or a can of chopped tomatoes
Pizza toppings from the fridge: ham, corn, peppers, olives, mushrooms
Five breads for Wednesday: sliced white, a seeded roll, a bagel, a pita, an English muffin
Two clean jars, one of them with a tight-fitting lid
A small rigid pot with a lid, for Kreston's scrap of dough
Clear plastic bottles, 2 × 500 ml, from the recycling
Balloons, 4 (two for the bottles, two spare)
An old baking tray and a plastic tub for the mud bakery
A wire rack, or a cold plate
A wooden spoon, a teaspoon, a serving spoon per person, a fork and a pastry brush
A table knife and a butter knife
A big board for cutting the pizzas on
A funnel, or paper to roll into a cone
A stool she can stand on
A permanent marker and a pen
A hole punch, or a stapler
A cereal box, flattened for a cover
Buttons or bottle tops, 30, and a coin purse
Fifty cents in coins for Thursday's thrift store
opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 8 months this week. He crawls or shuffles, brings two objects together to bang them, and checks your face before he decides what a new thing is for. He turns 8 months on Friday the 5th, the first day of the week, and stranger wariness arrives with it.

days.title: The Dough That Wakes Up
days.prepTonight: Set the flour, salt, sugar, two packets of active dry yeast and a clean jam jar on the table.

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Rolls and the Hollow Knock

opening.title: The Fizzing Jar
opening.need: 1 clean jam jar · active dry yeast, 1 packet · sugar, 1 tsp · warm water, 100 ml · 1 teaspoon.
steps: Fill the jar a third full, cold water in first and hot run in after, until it feels like bath water on your wrist. Let her test it with one finger.
Tip in the yeast and the sugar and let her stir. Then walk away for ten minutes.
Come back and look. The top has gone beige and foamy and smells of beer. Tell her the yeast is alive and has been eating the sugar.

main.title: Four Things Make Bread
materials: The jam jar of woken yeast from 8:00
steps: Count the four things on her fingers before anything goes in the bowl: flour, water, salt, yeast.

Flour into the bowl, salt to one side, and let her punch a well in the middle. The packet of yeast goes in the well, then the oil and the warm water. The jar of foam from 8:00 stands beside the bowl as the proof it is alive, and it goes down the sink at the end.
She mixes with one hand until it comes together as a shaggy lump. It sticks to her. Leave it sticking.
Turn it onto the table and knead: push with the heel of your hand, fold, turn a quarter, push again. Say the four words out loud and hand it over.
Ten minutes of that between you. She will manage two and wander off, so take it on and hand it back when she returns. The lump goes from ragged to smooth.
Oil the bowl, drop the dough in, cover it and stand it somewhere warm. Mark its height on the outside with a strip of tape.
main.tip: Kneading is heavy work and it settles a wound-up morning better than any instruction to calm down. Give her all ten minutes.

outside.title: The Walk Past the Bakery
paras: Walk to whichever store near you bakes on the premises. The supermarket counter counts. Cold February air holds the smell tight to the doorway, so the last four steps are the good ones. Count the shapes through the glass: rounds, long ones, braids, rolls with seeds. Buy one thing and let her carry it home in her own hand.

days.infant: Kreston turns 8 months today and he is crawling, which changes what a kitchen is. Set him up at the far end of the room with two metal spoons and a plastic bowl. Banging two objects together is new this month and needs both hands working to one plan. Say happy eight months out loud.

second.title: The Rolls and the Hollow Knock
second.intro: The dough has doubled by one o'clock and it holds the dent when she pushes a finger in.
materials: 2 tbsp milk and a pastry brush or a spoon
1 wire rack or a cold plate
Butter for the first one, eaten warm
steps: Tip the dough onto a floured table and let her press all the air out of it. It sighs down and she will want to do it twice.
Cut it into eight or ten pieces. She cuts, you even them up afterwards without saying so.
Show her the roll: hand cupped over the piece, palm circling, dough turning underneath. Hers come out as lumps and lumps bake fine.
Space them on the lined tray a hand's width apart, cover, and leave them thirty minutes. Oven on to 425°F.
Brush the tops with milk and bake fifteen to eighteen minutes. She watches through the glass and the door stays shut.
Out onto the rack. Once one has cooled enough to hold, turn it over and knock the bottom with a knuckle. Hollow means baked through, so let her knock every one.
Butter the first and eat it standing up in the kitchen before anyone suggests plates.
second.tip: Knock on a raw one before the tray goes in. She needs the dull thud at one thirty to hear the hollow one an hour later.

alternatives: A store-bought pack of dough, and skip to the knocking.
Shape the whole batch as one loaf and cut a cross in the top.
Roll long snakes and braid three of them together.
outAgain: A friend's house, and she carries a bag of the rolls to the door herself
The park, for the swings before the light goes
The corner store for butter and jam, both chosen by her
A café, where somebody else has done the baking
Back past the bakery window to see what has sold out

aroundWorld.title: Bread Everywhere 🥖
paras: Almost everywhere on earth makes a bread from the same short list. India tears naan off the wall of a clay oven. Mexico presses tortillas flat between two hands. Ethiopia ferments injera until it turns sour, and it works as the plate as well as the bread. France buys a baguette twice a day because it goes stale by evening.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Buy one bread you have never eaten, tear it at the table and eat it with your hands. Azlyn decides whether it beats her rolls.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: Injera is cooked on one side only, which is why the top is covered in tiny holes.

days.krestonPM: Kreston gets a soft roll with the crust off, torn small, sitting upright with you in front of him. Stranger wariness is arriving this month, so at the friend's house keep him on your hip for the first ten minutes. He comes off you when he leans off you and not before.

insight.headline: Auditory attention is trainable, and it underpins reading.
paras: Azlyn knocking the bottom of a roll and deciding whether it sounds hollow is doing fine listening work: two sounds held side by side, one picked out from the other. That skill sits underneath reading. Before she can match a letter to a sound she has to hear that bat and pat start with different mouths, and children who catch small differences in sound learn to read with less effort later on. Kitchens are good ground for it. The kettle, the fizzing jar, the knock on a crust, the oven timer. Name a sound out loud and she starts collecting them.

days.safety: Kreston is crawling and the oven runs at 425°F today, with hot trays coming out at his head height. Block his route to the oven door with a chair or the stroller before the dough goes in, and check it is still there before you open the door. Never leave the oven door open to cool with him loose in the room.

days.title: Azlyn's Own Recipe
days.prepTonight: Stand 100 g of butter out to soften overnight, and put the sugar and the all-purpose flour on the table beside it. The egg comes out of the fridge at breakfast.

opening.title: Choosing Off the Shelf
opening.need: the baking cupboard · a stool to stand on · paper and a pen.
steps: Open the cupboard and get her up to eye level with the shelf. Read out what is in each tub and let her hold the ones with lids.
She picks the additions for her recipe. If that is sprinkles and mashed banana together, it is sprinkles and mashed banana together.
Write her choices at the top of a fresh page under her name. Nothing gets vetoed.

main.title: The Recipe She Tells You
materials: Her chosen additions: raisins, chocolate chips, cocoa, sprinkles or a mashed banana
Paper and a pen for her words
steps: Sit down with her and ask how it is made, starting with the first thing into the bowl.
Write every word as it comes. And then you shake it a lot. Two hundred sugars. Do not tidy the order or fix the grammar.
Read it back from the top. She will change things. Cross out and write the new version underneath so both stay.
Now make it off her page. Quantities come from the list above, order comes from her.
Roll the mixture into walnut-sized balls, flatten them onto the lined tray with gaps between, and she adds her extras where her page says.
Bake at 350°F for twelve to fifteen minutes until the edges brown. Read her recipe out loud once more while they bake.
main.tip: Follow her order even where it makes a mess of the batch, and say out loud what happened. A batch that comes out odd beats one you fixed behind her back.

outside.title: The Frost Patch Hunt
paras: Go out before the sun reaches the shady side of the street. Frost survives where it has not: north-facing walls, the ground under parked cars, grass in the shadow of a hedge. Give her five patches to find and a fingernail to scratch each one. A mild night leaves you nothing white, so hunt the cold instead: the slab that stays dark, the dew standing on a car roof, the metal gate that stings her palm. Put her bare hand flat for one second, then back in the mitten.

days.infant: Kreston is 8 months and stranger wariness has landed, so the far end of the table will not do. Sit him where he can see your face while you write, with a wooden spoon and a plastic tub to bang together. Outside, hold his bare palm on the frost for a second and watch his face.

second.title: Her Page in the Cookbook
second.intro: This afternoon her recipe becomes a page in a book with her name on the front.
materials: The written recipe from this morning
1 cereal box cut flat for the cover
String and a hole punch, or a stapler
steps: Trim the sheets to a size her hands can turn and lay them in order.
Tape the morning's recipe onto the middle page, butter stain and crossings-out and all.
She draws one ingredient per sheet on the pages before it: butter, sugar, egg, flour, her own addition. Write the word underneath in your own hand, big.
Cut the cereal box flat for the cover and let her color it. Ask her the name of the book and write it across the front word for word.
Punch two holes down the left edge of every sheet and thread the string. Three staples down the spine work as well.
Read it back cover to cover, turning the pages at her pace.
Stand it on the kitchen shelf with the real cookbooks, at her height.
second.tip: She matches the shape of the word to the picture she made, and by Thursday she will find butter on the page unprompted.

alternatives: One page only, her drawing on one side and her words on the other.
Photograph each step of the morning and stick the photos in instead.
Add a page for a recipe she invents that nobody has to make.
outAgain: The museum, first Saturday of February and the second of the year
The indoor play center, if the parking lot beats you
The park, and a bag of yesterday's rolls if any survived
A café, and she orders her own thing out loud
The Saturday market, for a stall with something baked on it
days.krestonPM: Kreston goes in the carrier facing in today. At 8 months a museum is a room full of unfamiliar faces at his eye level, and your chest is where he turns back to between looks. Find one low thing with lights or a mirror and sit on the floor while he works it. Twenty-five minutes is a full visit.

insight.headline: Dictated stories are the bridge to real literacy.
paras: Azlyn cannot write and she can compose. Those two come apart at three, and taking her recipe down word for word lets the second run ahead of the first. She watches her own speech turn into marks you read back the same way twice, which is the idea underneath all of reading: the marks hold the words. Teachers call it language experience, and children who dictate to an adult arrive at writing with more to say and less fear of a blank page. Keep her wrong grammar in. Her sentence made the trip onto paper whole and comes back the same.

days.safety: Raw egg and raw flour both carry a real infection risk and she will eat some of the mixture. Hold it to one small spoonful, or set a spoonful aside before the egg goes in. Kreston gets none of it raw, and cookies are sugar all the way through, so he skips the baked ones too. The bowl goes in the sink and not on the floor. The oven runs at 350°F with him crawling, so block his route to the oven door with a chair or the stroller before the tray goes in, and check the block is still there before the tray comes out.

days.title: Pizza by Hand
days.prepTonight: Mix tonight's dough before bed (500 g bread flour, 7 g yeast, 1 tsp salt, 300 ml water, 1 tbsp oil), cover the bowl and leave it in the fridge to rise overnight.

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Long Bath After the Flour

opening.title: Punching It Down
opening.need: the overnight dough, cold from the fridge · flour · a dish towel.
steps: Take the bowl out and let her look first. The dough has climbed the sides overnight and smells sour.
Give her one instruction: fist in, all the way. The whole thing sighs to a third of its height and she will laugh.
Leave it under the dish towel to come to room temperature. Cold dough will not stretch, so the wait is an hour.

main.title: The Dough That Fights Back
materials: The overnight dough (500 g bread flour, 7 g yeast, 1 tsp salt, 300 ml water, 1 tbsp oil)
Or a 500 g pack of ready-made pizza dough, if last night got away from you
Flour for the table, a good handful
steps: Flour the table well. Cut the dough in half and give her one half.
Show her both flat hands pushing out from the middle, then work yours.
She will tear hers. Pinch it shut, carry on, and say out loud that dough mends and paper does not.
Once it is about tray-sized, lift an edge and let it hang from her hands. It stretches under its own weight and springs back when she lays it down. Let her try yours as well.
Lay both bases on the oiled trays and push them to the corners with her fingertips. Bumpy is right.
Cover them with the dish towel until one o'clock.
main.tip: Flour her hands and keep it off the dough. Flour worked in makes it tough, and hers has four hours of poking ahead of it.

outside.title: Stamping the Ice
paras: Take the route with puddles. February ice is thin and goes white where air got trapped underneath. It cracks under a boot with a sound she will chase down the path. Stamp one, then lift a plate of ice out of another and hold it against the sky. A mild week leaves the puddles open, so pick the deepest one instead and stand a stick in it to mark the water line. Wet gloves come home in a pocket.

days.infant: Kreston is 8 months and shuffling, so the floured floor is his now. Sweep before you put him down, then give him a scrap of dough shut in a small rigid pot with the lid taped on hard. Raw dough is dangerous eaten and a food bag is a suffocation risk at his age, so he gets the pot and never the bag, and it comes back the moment you stop watching. He shakes it, drops it and goes after it. On the walk, hold a plate of ice above the stroller for him.

second.title: One Pizza Each
second.intro: Everything comes to the table in small bowls at one o'clock and nobody builds anybody else's.
materials: Tomato sauce, or a can of chopped tomatoes
Whatever is in the fridge in small bowls: ham, corn, peppers, olives, mushrooms
steps: Set the bowls in a line down the table, a spoon standing in each.
Sauce first. Show her the spoon spiralling out from the middle, then let her do her own. The edges she misses stay missed.
Cheese by the handful. Everyone works down the line taking what they want, and nobody comments.
She will build yours as well. Eat whatever she puts on it.
Oven as hot as it goes, 475°F if you can get it. One tray at a time, top shelf, ten to twelve minutes, until the edges blister.
Out onto the board, herbs over the top, and cut hers into strips.
Eat at the table. This is Sunday lunch and the big meal of the day.
second.tip: Put one bowl out with something in it she has refused for a month. Sitting near a food, touching it and putting it back down is most of the road before she eats it.

alternatives: Store-bought bases or split pittas, same line of bowls.
One big pizza cut into pieces instead of one each.
Faces on the pizzas, built out of the toppings.
Sauce and cheese only, and no argument about the rest.
outAgain: The sunset walk, out at three for the long shadows, then back at the window by five when the sun goes
The park while the bases proof, if one o'clock ran late
A drive up to anywhere with a view west, and stay in the warm car
The duck pond, and back before the cold gets into her hands
Round the block counting the west-facing windows with the low sun in them
days.krestonPM: Kreston eats before the pizzas go in, then takes a strip of cooled plain base at the table. At 8 months he brings both hands and his gums to it and most of it ends up on the tray. Wrap him warm for the walk and use a hat with a chin strap, since a loose one is off his head inside a minute.

insight.headline: Cabin fever is a real physiological thing, not a bad attitude.
paras: Six weeks into winter, Azlyn is short of two things her body runs on: daylight and room to move. Morning light sets the clock that governs her sleep and her mood, and a February day indoors gives her a fraction of what an August one hands over. Add a body built to cover a few miles a day and a house that allows eight steps in a line, and the four o'clock meltdown reads as a shortage of both. Twenty minutes outside under flat gray cloud beats an hour under a lamp. Yours counts too, and you run the same shortage she does.

days.safety: The oven goes to 475°F today and Kreston is shuffling, so block his route to it with a chair or the stroller before the first tray goes in, and check the block is still there before you open the door. Melted cheese holds its heat long after the crust has cooled. Cut hers into strips and leave them three minutes on the board before the plate reaches her. If there is ice underfoot on the walk, take the salted side of the path and keep one hand free for her.

days.title: The Bakery Opens
days.prepTonight: Check the cupboard for half a kilo of all-purpose flour, a full tub of salt and the food coloring.

opening.title: Coloring the Dough
opening.need: all-purpose flour, 2 cups · salt, 1 cup · warm water, 1 cup · oil, 2 tbsp · food coloring · 1 big bowl.
steps: Flour and salt in the bowl, her hands in to mix them dry. Then oil and warm water, stirred until it leaves the sides.
Knead it on the table for two minutes while it is warm, then split it into three.
Press a hollow into each piece, three drops of a different color into each, and let her fold it in. Her hands come out patchy and wash clean by lunch.

main.title: Twelve Pretend Pastries
materials: No-cook playdough: 2 cups all-purpose flour, 1 cup salt, 1 cup warm water, 2 tbsp oil
1 rolling pin or a straight-sided glass
Paper cupcake liners, or squares of baking paper
1 baking tray as the display tray
steps: Line the tray with the cupcake liners first, so it looks like a store window.
Croissants: roll a ball, flatten it, cut a triangle, roll from the wide end and curve the ends in. Do one, hand her the knife, let hers come out fat.
Braids: three snakes rolled under her flat palms, pinched at the top and crossed over one another.
Buns and rings: balls pressed with the back of the fork, and snakes joined end to end for doughnuts.
Keep going until the tray is full. Count them on out loud, one to twelve, then backwards when the dough runs out.
Stand the tray on the counter you are about to build. None of it gets baked and she will ask twice.
main.tip: Make one wrong on purpose. She corrects you, and correcting an adult's croissant buys her more practice than praise ever will.

outside.title: The Mud Bakery
paras: Take an old baking tray, a wooden spoon and a plastic tub to the muddiest patch you can reach. February mud is soft to the top of a boot and cold enough to hold a shape. She makes mud pastries to match the ones on the kitchen counter and counts them the same way. Leave them there for the frost.

days.infant: Kreston is 8 months and everything reachable goes to his mouth on its way to being understood, so the pastry tray lives above his line all day. Give him a whole sheet of baking paper instead, too big to get into his mouth. He crushes it, drops it, hears it land and leans over to look.

second.title: The Counter Opens
second.intro: A dining chair turned side-on is the counter. She takes the inside, you take the sidewalk side and the customer's part for the afternoon.
materials: 1 small table or a chair as the counter
Paper and a marker for price signs
A coin purse of buttons or bottle tops as coins
steps: Set the counter where she says. Tray on top, shoebox register beside it, dish towel in her waistband as the apron.
Write the price signs with her, a number and a drawing on each, and she decides every number.
Be the first customer. Say good morning, ask for two things by name and wait for her to name a price.
Pay in buttons, one at a time, counted out loud into her hand. She puts them in the register and shuts the lid.
Bag the order and let it take as long as it takes. Folding the top over twice is the part she will want again.
Swap over. She comes in with the coin purse and you get one item of her order wrong on purpose.
Closing time at two thirty. Count the buttons out of the register, cover the tray and turn the sign round.
second.tip: Stay in role when she goes off script. If a croissant costs a hundred buttons, count out a hundred. Stepping out to explain money ends the game.

alternatives: Carry the tray round the house and sell door to door.
Line the pastries up by size and photograph the window.
One customer, one order, then she runs it on her own.
outAgain: The field walk, boots on, with the far hedge as the turning point
The neighborhood park, if the field is under water
One lap of the block with a paper bag, delivering to nobody
The green space with a ball, after an hour behind a counter
The yard with a bucket of water, poured over the mud pastries
days.krestonPM: Kreston is a customer. Sit him on your lap at the counter and let Azlyn hand him an empty paper bag, which he chews and then waves at her. At 8 months he checks your face to work out what a new thing is for, so take it back with a big thank you.

insight.headline: Pretend play is where self-control gets built.
paras: Azlyn behind that counter holds a rule in her head, and she holds it longer than she holds one of yours. That might be ten minutes or twenty, depending on the morning. Shopkeepers wait. They hand the bag over. They leave the stock alone. Nobody is enforcing any of it and she does it anyway, because the role says so. Children in role play stand still longer, wait longer and stay with a dull job longer than the same children asked to do the same thing without the pretend. Every minute she spends being a baker is practice at what you will want at five, in a classroom.

days.safety: Playdough carries far more salt than food and Kreston will have it in his mouth the second he is near the tray. Keep the tray above his reach and wipe the table before he goes on the floor. Buttons and bottle tops are choking-sized for an 8-month-old. Count them into the coin purse at the start and back into the register at closing.

days.title: What Yeast Eats
days.prepTonight: Rinse two 500 ml plastic bottles from the recycling, stand them upside down to dry, and find two balloons that have not perished.

opening.title: The Bath-Water Test
opening.need: 2 cups or mugs · the cold tap and the hot · 1 pitcher.
steps: Fill one cup from the cold tap. Fill the second with cold first, then run the hot in until it feels like bath water on your wrist.
She puts a finger in each and gives both a word. Warm as a bath is what yeast wants and anything hotter kills it.
Pour the warm one into the pitcher and stand it on the side. It goes into the bottles at 9:15.

main.title: The Balloon That Fills Itself
materials: 2 clear plastic bottles, 500 ml, from the recycling
Warm water from the morning test
1 funnel, or a cone rolled from paper
1 permanent marker for the level line
steps: Stand the bottles side by side and let her mark them 1 and 2.
Bottle 1 gets a packet of yeast and a teaspoon of sugar down the funnel, then warm water. Bottle 2 gets warm water only. Draw a line on both at the same height.
She swirls bottle 1 until the yeast clouds the water. Bottle 2 gets the same swirling and stays clear.
Stretch a balloon over each neck, right down over the shoulder so it grips.
Stand them somewhere warm and look at the clock together, then go outside.
Back at eleven thirty, bottle 1's balloon stands up and bottle 2's is flat. Let her squeeze both and ask which had food in it.
main.tip: Draw round each balloon on paper at ten thirty and again at eleven thirty. Two outlines on one page make an hour of slow change visible to her.

outside.title: The First Birdsong Walk
paras: Cardinals and chickadees start up again in the second week of February, and a street with no leaves on it carries the sound a long way. Give her a number and walk until she has counted twenty songs. Stand still for each one and let her point at the roof or the branch it came from before you move on. A cold, still morning gives you the most of it.

days.infant: Kreston is 8 months and bangs two things together with real intent this month. Give him two plastic cups at the far end of the room while the bottles work. He brings them together, misses, brings them together again, and the miss is the part he works on.

second.title: Shaking Cream into Butter
second.intro: A jar, a tight lid, and everybody in the house taking a turn.
materials: Heavy cream, 300 ml, out of the fridge an hour before
1 clean jar with a tight-fitting lid
A cold plate for the butter
steps: Pour the cream in until the jar is half full, no further, so there is air above it. Screw the lid down hard and check it twice.
Everybody shakes. Count to fifty each and pass it on. Azlyn's fifty will be short and loud and she gets all the turns she wants.
Around five minutes in it goes thick and the sloshing stops. That is whipped cream, and she is halfway.
Keep going through the quiet stretch. The sound comes back as a heavier thud, then a lump rolling round in liquid. Open the jar and let her look.
Strain it through the sieve over the bowl. The lump is butter, the liquid is buttermilk and she can drink some.
Squeeze the butter under cold water with the back of a spoon until it runs clear, work in the salt and press it onto the cold plate.
Spread it on bread and eat it at the counter. The rest goes in the fridge for tomorrow.
second.tip: Sit on the floor and pass the jar back and forth. The passing keeps her in it once her arms have gone.

alternatives: Whipped cream only, and stop while it is still cream.
Taste the buttermilk against the milk in the fridge.
Butter on toast, jam on top, nothing else asked of anyone.
outAgain: Swimming
The indoor play center, if the school lessons have the pool
The library a day early, for a book with bread in it
A warm café and a window seat
The park, for ten minutes on the swings before the light goes
days.krestonPM: Kreston comes to the pool. At 8 months he sits supported in the water and slaps at it with a flat hand for the full twenty minutes. Hold him chest to chest facing you at first, because a changing room full of voices is a lot to take. Out and dressed before he cools.

insight.headline: Regression during illness is expected, not a setback.
paras: Azlyn will catch something this month, and when she does she will want feeding, carrying and sleeping next to you, and things she has managed on her own since the autumn will stop. Skills built in the last few months sit on top of a lot of effort, and a body spending everything it has on fighting a virus takes that effort back first. Sleep goes, then the toilet, then the words. Give her what she asks for while she is ill. Children who get the extra holding return to where they were within a week or two of getting well.

days.safety: Balloons are the worst choking hazard in this house for an 8-month-old, whole or burst, and a burst piece molds to the airway where nothing can shift it. Keep the spares in your pocket, count them out and count them back in, and throw away any that split. Run the cold in first and test the water on your wrist before her finger goes near it, because a hot tap on its own will scald. At the pool stay within arm's reach of both of them, and that means arm's reach and not eyeline.

days.title: Five Kinds of Bread
days.prepTonight: Put the five breads out (sliced white, a seeded roll, a bagel, a pita, an English muffin) with five plates, the marker or the sticky labels and the bread knife beside them.

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: One Slow Lap of the Block

opening.title: Numbering the Plates
opening.need: 5 plates · 1 marker or 5 sticky labels · the five breads · a bread knife (adult).
steps: Lay the five plates in a row and let her put a number on each. Write yours underneath hers if the numbers come out as shapes.
You cut and she plates. One piece of each bread onto its own numbered plate, each piece the size of a bite.
Cover the whole row with a dish towel and walk away. She will lift the corner twice before nine.

main.title: Which Bread Wins
materials: Five breads: sliced white, a seeded roll, a bagel, a pita or tortilla, an English muffin
5 plates and a marker for the numbers
Paper and crayons for the chart
steps: Sit her down with the row in front of her and the cup of water beside it.
Plate 1 first. One bite, chew, a mouthful of water, then talk about it before plate 2 comes near her.
Ask what her tongue found. Soft, crunchy, holey, chewy, seedy. Write her word next to the number, and hers will include spiky and like a pillow.
Work along to plate 5 with water between each one. No doubling back until the row is finished.
Hand her the stickers or a crayon. Every bread she would eat again gets a mark, as many as she likes.
Count the marks together and say the winner out loud, then eat the rest of it with yesterday's butter.
main.tip: Give your own answers as you go and say so when yours differ from hers. A tasting where the adult has a favorite stays a conversation.

outside.title: One Slow Lap of the Block
paras: Walk the block at her pace, which turns a five-minute loop into twenty, and let her set every stop. This is the week the buds show on the hedges, hard little points on bare stems, so put her fingers on one and then on a bare stem. Count the front doors down one side and look over every fence for the first green thing in anybody's yard.

days.infant: Kreston is 8 months and he gets his own plate at the end of the row. Soft white bread with the crust off, torn into thumb-sized pieces, and he sits upright at the table with you in front of him. He rakes food in with a whole fist, so expect most of the plate down his front.

second.title: The Bakery Window
second.intro: The front window faces the street. Fill it from the inside and the house reads as a bakery to anyone walking past.
materials: A marker for the shop name she chooses
steps: Lay the paper out and start with loaves. Show her the long shape and the round shape once each, then leave her to it.
Buns, braids, cakes with something on top. Big drawings work better in a window than accurate ones.
Cut each one out along her line while she draws the next. She fills sheets faster than you can cut.
Ask her the name of the shop. Write it across a sheet in fat marker, saying each letter as you make it.
Tape the sign up first, top of the window, facing out to the street.
She decides where every item goes and you do the taping. Put a row at her eye level.
Coats on, out onto the sidewalk, and stand across the road looking back at the house. It takes four minutes.
second.tip: Facing out means the drawings are backwards from the inside. Say so before she notices, and let her draw two of one thing so there is one pointing each way.

alternatives: The fridge door instead of the window, and no cutting out.
One big drawing of the whole shop on the back of a cereal box.
Cut bread pictures out of a supermarket magazine and put those up.
outAgain: The church hall playgroup, and she can tell somebody about the window
The library, if the hall is shut this week
The indoor play center, if the playgroup crowd is more than either of you wants
A walk past the front of the house so she sees her own window from the street
The store for tomorrow's cinnamon, chosen and carried by her
days.krestonPM: Kreston stays on you at playgroup longer than he did in January. Stranger wariness is at its peak and a hall of unfamiliar adults at knee height is the thing it exists for. Find a corner with a mat and sit there rather than passing him round. He lets go once the hall has stopped being new.

insight.headline: Boredom on the mend is a good sign, and a useful one.
paras: Two days flat on the sofa with a virus, and then Azlyn starts complaining that there is nothing to do. That complaint is the first clean signal her body has finished the job. It is also the most useful hour of your week: a child with nothing arranged has to reach for her own idea, and the reaching is the whole skill. Sit with the whining for ten minutes without solving it. Suggest nothing and carry on with what you were doing. Most of the time she starts something you would never have thought of, and it holds her twice as long as anything you set up.

days.safety: No honey for Kreston before he is one. Infant botulism is rare and serious, and honey turns up in seeded loaves, malted bread and English muffin toppings, so read the bag. Seeds, crusts and torn bagel are all choking-sized for him at 8 months, so his plate is soft white with the crust off and nothing else.

days.title: Delivery Day
days.prepTonight: Make tonight's dough before bed (500 g bread flour, 7 g yeast, 1 tsp salt, 300 ml water, 1 tbsp oil) and leave it covered in the fridge, or buy a pack instead. Stand 75 g of butter out on the counter to soften, and put whatever card and colored paper you own somewhere findable for next week.

opening.title: The Cinnamon Butter
opening.need: soft butter, 75 g · sugar, 75 g · ground cinnamon, 2 tsp · 1 small bowl · 1 fork · her cookbook from Saturday.
steps: Stand her cookbook open at the butter page and let her find the word. Butter, sugar and cinnamon into the bowl, and she mashes it to a brown paste.
Let her smell the bowl, then the jar on its own. The jar is sharper and she will pull a face.
Cover it and leave it on the side. Wash the fork before the mixture sets.

main.title: The Swirl Buns
materials: Bread or pizza dough, made last night, or a shop-bought pack
A length of dental floss, or a table knife
1 round cake pan or a baking tray
steps: Flour the table and roll the dough into a rectangle the size of a dish towel. She leans on the pin, you finish the corners.
She spreads the cinnamon butter to the edges with the back of a spoon. All of it goes on.
Roll it up from the long side into a tight log, her hands on top of yours.
Slide the floss under the log, cross the ends and pull. Cut twelve and let her count them into the pan.
Space them with room to grow, cover, and leave them somewhere warm for forty minutes.
Walk the round while they prove, then bake at 375°F for twenty-five minutes until the tops brown, with you in the kitchen the whole time. Out and cooling by twelve.
main.tip: Cut the log with floss. A knife squashes the spiral flat, and the spiral is why she is up on that stool.

outside.title: Walking the Round Empty-Handed
paras: Walk the delivery round before there is anything to deliver. Stop outside each house, say who lives there and let her say it back and pick the door out. February yards give her nothing to go on, so use what stands out: the red door, the van, the cat in the window.

days.infant: Kreston is 8 months and follows the smell of the oven across the floor now. Put him in the high chair with the scraped-out cinnamon bowl and a wooden spoon, near enough to watch her roll. He bangs them together and looks at you to see whether that was allowed.

second.title: The Four Boxes
second.intro: Twelve buns, four names, four boxes, and she decides what goes where.
materials: 4 small boxes or paper bags from the recycling
Paper for the labels and a card each
steps: Lay the boxes out and let her pick one for each person, saying the names aloud.
She colors each box for the person it is going to. The neighbor's takes twice as long.
Write the names big on the labels while she watches, saying the letters. She tapes each onto the right box.
Cut a card for each and let her make her mark inside. Ask what it says and write her words underneath.
Line the boxes with baking paper and load them, two buns each. She decides who gets the biggest, and the last four stay here.
Tie the string round and knot it, her hands over yours.
Deliver at two o'clock on the round you walked this morning. She carries one box to the door and hands it over. Stay two steps back.
second.tip: Ring the bell and say nothing. She has rehearsed this all morning and she will get the words out if the gap is long enough.

alternatives: Paper bags instead of boxes, and stop after the names go on.
One box for one person, and a longer walk to get there.
Drop the cards through the mail slots and keep the buns.
Draw the round as a map on a flattened box, houses in order.
outAgain: The thrift store, and she has fifty cents of her own for one thing off the shelf
The rest of the delivery round, if this afternoon ran long and there are doors left
The park on the way home, with a bun in a bag
The corner store, and she hands over the money for the milk
A walk to the mailbox with a card for somebody too far to deliver to
days.krestonPM: Kreston does the round in the stroller, wrapped, with the boxes at his feet. At 8 months a door opening onto a new face is the entire event, so give him a second at each one. In the thrift store keep him on you, since the aisles are narrow and the shelves sit at grab height.

insight.headline: On the days you use this page instead of the plan.
paras: Some mornings the plan is wrong. He was up four times, she is off, and the page is asking for an oven and ninety minutes. Do one thing off the Afternoon Alternatives instead, or none of it, and put a movie on. A day where Azlyn ate, got outside for twenty minutes and had you within reach is a day that did her good. Warm, responsive, unhurried adults are what the early childhood research keeps coming back to, and nothing printed on this page outranks them. The book is a menu on those days, written by somebody who was not in the room.

days.safety: The floss and the string go back in the drawer the moment the cutting and the tying are done. A loose length of either is a strangulation risk at 8 months and Kreston is on the floor all afternoon. The pan comes out of a 375°F oven, so stand it at the back of the counter where he cannot pull it down, and give it an hour before anyone lifts it bare-handed. Put Azlyn on the stool for the rolling rather than a dining chair, since she leans her whole weight onto that pin.
